claim: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a major component of tumors and a significant contributor to cancer progression.
source: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a major component of tumors and a significant contributor to cancer progression.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about ECM's role in cancer.

claim: Primary tumors of differing metastatic potential differ in ECM composition.
source: In this study, we use proteomics to investigate the ECM of human mammary carcinoma xenografts and show that primary tumors of differing metastatic potential differ in ECM composition.
evidence: This claim is supported by the proteomic analysis data presented in the manuscript showing different ECM protein profiles between MDA-MB-231 and LM2 tumors.

claim: Both tumor cells and stromal cells contribute to the tumor matrix.
source: Both tumor cells and stromal cells contribute to the tumor matrix and tumors of differing metastatic ability differ in both tumor- and stroma-derived ECM components.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data distinguishing human (tumor) from mouse (stroma) peptides.

claim: Tumors of differing metastatic ability differ in both tumor- and stroma-derived ECM components.
source: Both tumor cells and stromal cells contribute to the tumor matrix and tumors of differing metastatic ability differ in both tumor- and stroma-derived ECM components.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the species-specific peptide analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: ECM signatures of poorly and highly metastatic mammary carcinomas reveal up-regulation of signaling pathways including TGFβ and VEGF.
source: We define ECM signatures of poorly and highly metastatic mammary carcinomas and these signatures reveal up-regulation of signaling pathways including TGFβ and VEGF.
evidence: This is supported by the Ingenuity Pathway Analysis results shown in Figure 4.

claim: LTBP3 plays a causal role in metastasis.
source: We further demonstrate that several proteins characteristic of highly metastatic tumors (LTBP3, SNED1, EGLN1, and S100A2) play causal roles in metastasis, albeit at different steps.
evidence: This is demonstrated by knockdown experiments showing reduced metastasis when LTBP3 is knocked down.

claim: SNED1 plays a causal role in metastasis.
source: We further demonstrate that several proteins characteristic of highly metastatic tumors (LTBP3, SNED1, EGLN1, and S100A2) play causal roles in metastasis, albeit at different steps.
evidence: This is demonstrated by knockdown experiments showing reduced metastasis when SNED1 is knocked down.

claim: EGLN1 plays a causal role in metastasis.
source: We further demonstrate that several proteins characteristic of highly metastatic tumors (LTBP3, SNED1, EGLN1, and S100A2) play causal roles in metastasis, albeit at different steps.
evidence: This is demonstrated by knockdown experiments showing reduced metastasis when EGLN1 is knocked down.

claim: S100A2 plays a causal role in metastasis.
source: We further demonstrate that several proteins characteristic of highly metastatic tumors (LTBP3, SNED1, EGLN1, and S100A2) play causal roles in metastasis, albeit at different steps.
evidence: This is demonstrated by knockdown experiments showing reduced metastasis when S100A2 is knocked down.

claim: High expression of LTBP3 correlates with poor outcome for ER−/PR− breast cancer patients.
source: Finally we show that high expression of LTBP3 and SNED1 correlates with poor outcome for ER−/PR−breast cancer patients.
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: High expression of SNED1 correlates with poor outcome for ER−/PR− breast cancer patients.
source: Finally we show that high expression of LTBP3 and SNED1 correlates with poor outcome for ER−/PR−breast cancer patients.
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Breast cancer is the second most frequent cancer worldwide with an estimated 1.3 million new cases in 2008.
source: With an estimated number of new cases in 2008 of 1.3 million worldwide (http://globocan.iarc.fr), breast cancer is the second most frequent cancer worldwide and claimed the lives of over 39,000 patients in the United States in 2012 alone.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the globocan.iarc.fr database.

claim: Breast cancer claimed the lives of over 39,000 patients in the United States in 2012.
source: With an estimated number of new cases in 2008 of 1.3 million worldwide (http://globocan.iarc.fr), breast cancer is the second most frequent cancer worldwide and claimed the lives of over 39,000 patients in the United States in 2012 alone.
evidence: This is a factual statement about cancer mortality statistics.

claim: Most cancer deaths (∼90%) are due to the metastatic colonization of distant organs by the tumor cells.
source: Most cancer deaths (∼90%) are due to the metastatic colonization of distant organs by the tumor cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cancer biology.

claim: The tumor microenvironment encompasses all the components (cellular and acellular) of a tumor in addition to the tumor cells themselves.
source: For the last decade, there has been increasing interest in the tumor microenvironment, which encompasses all the components (cellular and acellular) of a tumor in addition to the tumor cells themselves (Joyce and Pollard, 2009; Egeblad et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Joyce and Pollard, 2009 and Egeblad et al., 2010.

claim: A tumor needs to be surrounded by a permissive environment in order to progress.
source: Indeed, in order to progress, a tumor needs to be surrounded by a permissive environment and, to metastasize, tumor cells need to find or create a favorable niche (seed and soil theory) (Paget, 1889; Ribatti et al., 2006; Erler and Weaver, 2009; Comen, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including the historical seed and soil theory.

claim: To metastasize, tumor cells need to find or create a favorable niche.
source: Indeed, in order to progress, a tumor needs to be surrounded by a permissive environment and, to metastasize, tumor cells need to find or create a favorable niche (seed and soil theory) (Paget, 1889; Ribatti et al., 2006; Erler and Weaver, 2009; Comen, 2012).
evidence: This is the seed and soil theory supported by citations.

claim: The cross-talk and interaction of breast tumor cells with their surrounding microenvironment is necessary for tumor progression.
source: In the context of breast cancer, recent studies have shown that the cross-talk and interaction of the tumor cells with their surrounding microenvironment is necessary for tumor progression (Tlsty and Coussens, 2006; Polyak et al., 2009; Dvorak et al., 2011; Boudreau et al., 2012; Conklin and Keely, 2012; Fordyce et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: The nature of the tumor microenvironment or gene expression profile of the stromal cells has been used to define human breast cancer types.
source: In addition, the nature of the tumor microenvironment or gene expression profile of the stromal cells has been used to define human breast cancer types (Bergamaschi et al., 2008; Finak et al., 2008; Conklin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bergamaschi et al., 2008; Finak et al., 2008; Conklin et al., 2011.

claim: Treatment outcome depends on the tumor microenvironment.
source: Recent studies have also demonstrated that treatment outcome depends on the tumor microenvironment (vascularization, oxygenation, recruited normal cells, etc; Chauhan et al., 2011; Jacobetz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chauhan et al., 2011 and Jacobetz et al., 2013.

claim: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is the complex scaffold of proteins that provides the architectural support for cell and tissue organization.
source: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is the complex scaffold of proteins that provides the architectural support for cell and tissue organization (Hynes and Naba, 2012).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to Hynes and Naba, 2012.

claim: Cells are able to adhere to the extracellular matrix via different types of receptors including the integrins.
source: Cells are in turn able to adhere to the extracellular matrix via different types of receptors including the integrins (Hynes, 2002; Geiger and Yamada, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hynes, 2002 and Geiger and Yamada, 2011.

claim: The ECM provides biochemical signals that are major regulators of cell proliferation, survival, migration, and invasion.
source: In addition to providing biophysical cues, the ECM provides biochemical signals that are major regulators of cell proliferation, survival, migration, and invasion. (Hynes, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hynes, 2009.

claim: Pathologists have used excessive ECM deposition (desmoplasia) as a marker of tumors with poor prognosis.
source: Pathologists have used excessive ECM deposition (desmoplasia) as a marker of tumors with poor prognosis long before the complexity of the ECM was even deciphered (Anastassiades and Pryce, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Anastassiades and Pryce, 1974.

claim: The matrisome is defined as the ensemble of ECM and ECM-associated proteins.
source: To define the composition of extracellular matrices of tissues and tumors, we have developed a proteomics-based method to enrich and identify ECM proteins and coupled it with a bioinformatic annotation of the 'matrisome' defined as the ensemble of ECM and ECM-associated proteins (Naba et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a definition from the authors' previous work cited as Naba et al., 2012.

claim: Normal murine tissues (e.g., lung and colon) each comprise over 100 ECM proteins.
source: Using this approach, we characterized the extracellular matrices of normal murine tissues (e.g., lung and colon) and demonstrated that each of these comprises over 100 proteins.
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous proteomic characterization work.

claim: The poorly metastatic MDA-MB-231 cell line was established from cells isolated from a pleural effusion sample from a triple-negative breast cancer patient.
source: The poorly metastatic MDA-MB-231 cell line was established from cells isolated from a pleural effusion sample from a triple-negative breast cancer patient (Cailleau et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cailleau et al., 1978.

claim: The highly metastatic MDA-MB-231-LM2 line was previously selected and characterized for increased metastatic potential to the lungs.
source: The highly metastatic MDA-MB-231-LM2 line (denoted LM2), was previously selected and characterized for increased metastatic potential to the lungs (Minn et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Minn et al., 2005.

claim: The matrisome of MDA-MB-231 tumors is composed of 144 proteins.
source: According to this definition, the matrisome of MDA-MB-231 tumors is composed of 144 proteins and the matrisome of LM2 tumors is composed of 161 proteins (Figure 1B, Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in Figure 1B and Figure 2.

claim: The matrisome of LM2 tumors is composed of 161 proteins.
source: According to this definition, the matrisome of MDA-MB-231 tumors is composed of 144 proteins and the matrisome of LM2 tumors is composed of 161 proteins (Figure 1B, Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in Figure 1B and Figure 2.

claim: 118 proteins are expressed by both MDA-MB-231 and LM2 tumor types.
source: Comparison of the matrisomes of MDA-MB-231 and LM2 tumors identified 118 proteins expressed by both tumor types.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B Venn diagram.

claim: 26 proteins are specific to poorly metastatic (MDA-MB-231) tumors.
source: In addition, we detected 26 proteins specific to the poorly metastatic tumors and 43 proteins specific to highly metastatic tumors (Figure 1B, Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B Venn diagram.

claim: 43 proteins are specific to highly metastatic (LM2) tumors.
source: In addition, we detected 26 proteins specific to the poorly metastatic tumors and 43 proteins specific to highly metastatic tumors (Figure 1B, Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B Venn diagram.

claim: The most abundant proteins for each matrisome category were detected in both tumor types.
source: One can note that the most abundant proteins for each of these categories were detected in both tumor types.
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Fibronectin (FN1), fibrinogen, laminins, HSPG2 or perlecan, collagens I, III, IV, V and VI, and transglutaminase 2 (TGM2) are abundant proteins detected in both tumor types.
source: Examples of these proteins are fibronectin (FN1), fibrinogen, laminins, HSPG2 or perlecan, collagens I, III, IV, V and VI, and transglutaminase 2 (TGM2).
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Fibronectin, fibrinogen, laminins, HSPG2, collagens I, III, IV, V and VI, and TGM2 have been previously reported to be expressed in several normal tissues.
source: In fact, we have previously reported the expression of these proteins in several normal tissues (Naba et al., 2012), which suggests that these proteins are widely expressed.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Most of the matrisome-associated components were detected at lower abundance, reflecting their presence at lower molar ratios than structural core ECM proteins.
source: Most of the matrisome-associated components were detected at lower abundance, reflecting their presence at lower molar ratios than structural core ECM proteins (Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The proteins that differ between the two tumor types belong mostly to the ECM glycoproteins and the ECM regulators categories.
source: Therefore, the analysis identified ECM signatures of poorly (26 proteins) or highly (43 proteins) metastatic tumors (Figures 1B and 2) and the proteins that differ between the two tumor types belong mostly to the ECM glycoproteins and the ECM regulators categories.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the data in Figures 1B and 2.

claim: Angiopoietin-like 4 (ANGPTL4) has been previously reported to play a role in breast cancer metastasis.
source: Among the 43 proteins characteristic of highly metastatic tumors (Figure 3D), we identified several proteins that have previously been reported to play a role in breast cancer metastasis in diverse cell and tumor models. Examples of these are angiopoietin-like 4 (ANGPTL4, Padua et al., 2008), cathepsin B (CTSB, Sevenich et al., 2010, 2011; Vasiljeva et al., 2006), insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 4 (IGFBP4, Ryan et al., 2009) and lysyl-oxidase-like 2 (LOXL2, Barry-Hamilton et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Padua et al., 2008.

claim: Cathepsin B (CTSB) has been previously reported to play a role in breast cancer metastasis.
source: Among the 43 proteins characteristic of highly metastatic tumors (Figure 3D), we identified several proteins that have previously been reported to play a role in breast cancer metastasis in diverse cell and tumor models. Examples of these are angiopoietin-like 4 (ANGPTL4, Padua et al., 2008), cathepsin B (CTSB, Sevenich et al., 2010, 2011; Vasiljeva et al., 2006), insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 4 (IGFBP4, Ryan et al., 2009) and lysyl-oxidase-like 2 (LOXL2, Barry-Hamilton et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sevenich et al., 2010, 2011 and Vasiljeva et al., 2006.

claim: Insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 4 (IGFBP4) has been previously reported to play a role in breast cancer metastasis.
source: Among the 43 proteins characteristic of highly metastatic tumors (Figure 3D), we identified several proteins that have previously been reported to play a role in breast cancer metastasis in diverse cell and tumor models. Examples of these are angiopoietin-like 4 (ANGPTL4, Padua et al., 2008), cathepsin B (CTSB, Sevenich et al., 2010, 2011; Vasiljeva et al., 2006), insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 4 (IGFBP4, Ryan et al., 2009) and lysyl-oxidase-like 2 (LOXL2, Barry-Hamilton et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2009.

claim: Lysyl-oxidase-like 2 (LOXL2) has been previously reported to play a role in breast cancer metastasis.
source: Among the 43 proteins characteristic of highly metastatic tumors (Figure 3D), we identified several proteins that have previously been reported to play a role in breast cancer metastasis in diverse cell and tumor models. Examples of these are angiopoietin-like 4 (ANGPTL4, Padua et al., 2008), cathepsin B (CTSB, Sevenich et al., 2010, 2011; Vasiljeva et al., 2006), insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 4 (IGFBP4, Ryan et al., 2009) and lysyl-oxidase-like 2 (LOXL2, Barry-Hamilton et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barry-Hamilton et al., 2010.

claim: 17 of the 43 ECM proteins found to be up-regulated in LM2 tumors are downstream of the TGFβ signaling pathway.
source: We found that 17 of the 43 (nearly 40%) ECM proteins found to be up-regulated in LM2 tumors are downstream of the TGFβ signaling pathway (Figure 4, left panel).
evidence: This is based on Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The majority of ECM proteins downstream of TGFβ are tumor-derived.
source: The majority of these are tumor-derived, although several host proteins (C1qa, C1qc and Vwf) are also identified as being downstream of TGFβ.
evidence: This is based on the species-specific peptide analysis and pathway analysis.

claim: The LM2 cell line and its metastatic potential have previously been shown to be dependent on TGFβ.
source: Interestingly, the LM2 cell line and its metastatic potential have previously been shown to be dependent on TGFβ (Minn et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Minn et al., 2007.

claim: 10 of the 43 ECM proteins identified in the study are influenced by the HIF1α/VEGF pathway.
source: One of the other signaling pathways significantly represented within our data set is the HIF1α/VEGF pathway that influences the levels of 10 of the 43 ECM proteins identified in our study (Figure 4, right panel).
evidence: This is based on Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is a large overlap between the targets of TGFβ and HIF1α/VEGF pathways.
source: We also noted that there is a large overlap between the targets of TGFβ and HIF1α/VEGF as the genes identified as being downstream of the HIF1α/VEGF pathway are all also downstream of the TGFβ pathway.
evidence: This is an observation from the pathway analysis data in Figure 4.

claim: The convergence of TGFβ and HIF1α signaling pathways is a key contributor to the cross-talk between breast tumor cells and stromal cells.
source: Interestingly, a recent publication by Curran and Keely highlights the convergence of TGFβ and HIF1α signaling pathways as a key contributor to the cross-talk between breast tumor cells and stromal cells (Curran and Keely, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Curran and Keely, 2013.

claim: By interrogating the tumor extracellular matrix, one can identify signaling pathways up-regulated within the tumor cells or stromal cells.
source: Altogether, this analysis indicates that by interrogating the tumor extracellular matrix, one can identify signaling pathways up-regulated within the tumor cells or stromal cells and these represent potential targets for therapeutic intervention.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pathway analysis results.

claim: LTBP3 was detected only in highly metastatic tumors.
source: Accordingly, we selected a set of proteins (LTBP3—Latent TGFβ Binding Protein 3; SNED1—Sushi, Nidogen and EGF-like Domains 1; EGLN1—Egl Nine homolog 1 and S100A2) based on the following criteria: they were (1) detected only in highly metastatic tumors; (2) secreted exclusively by the tumor cells; (3) in relatively high abundance (Figures 2 and 3D, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 1); (4) not previously investigated for any roles in metastasis.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figures 2 and 3D.

claim: SNED1 was detected only in highly metastatic tumors.
source: Accordingly, we selected a set of proteins (LTBP3—Latent TGFβ Binding Protein 3; SNED1—Sushi, Nidogen and EGF-like Domains 1; EGLN1—Egl Nine homolog 1 and S100A2) based on the following criteria: they were (1) detected only in highly metastatic tumors; (2) secreted exclusively by the tumor cells; (3) in relatively high abundance (Figures 2 and 3D, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 1); (4) not previously investigated for any roles in metastasis.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figures 2 and 3D.

claim: EGLN1 was detected only in highly metastatic tumors.
source: Accordingly, we selected a set of proteins (LTBP3—Latent TGFβ Binding Protein 3; SNED1—Sushi, Nidogen and EGF-like Domains 1; EGLN1—Egl Nine homolog 1 and S100A2) based on the following criteria: they were (1) detected only in highly metastatic tumors; (2) secreted exclusively by the tumor cells; (3) in relatively high abundance (Figures 2 and 3D, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 1); (4) not previously investigated for any roles in metastasis.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figures 2 and 3D.

claim: S100A2 was detected only in highly metastatic tumors.
source: Accordingly, we selected a set of proteins (LTBP3—Latent TGFβ Binding Protein 3; SNED1—Sushi, Nidogen and EGF-like Domains 1; EGLN1—Egl Nine homolog 1 and S100A2) based on the following criteria: they were (1) detected only in highly metastatic tumors; (2) secreted exclusively by the tumor cells; (3) in relatively high abundance (Figures 2 and 3D, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 1); (4) not previously investigated for any roles in metastasis.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figures 2 and 3D.

claim: CYR61 is a tumor-derived ECM protein detected in both MDA-MB-231 and LM2 tumors but with much greater abundance in LM2 tumors.
source: We also investigated the role of CYR61, a tumor-derived ECM protein detected in both MDA-MB-231 and LM2 tumors but with a much greater abundance in LM2 tumors (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on the proteomic data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: mRNA levels and steady-state protein levels do not correlate well.
source: We also performed RT-qPCR analyses for several other proteins in our lists despite the fact that it is well known that mRNA levels and steady-state protein levels do not correlate at all well (Gygi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gygi et al., 1999.

claim: The mRNA changes for CYR61, EGLN1, and LTBP3 do not show mRNA changes corresponding with the marked differences in protein levels detected.
source: It can be seen that the mRNA changes for several of the proteins of interest (CYR61, EGLN1, LTBP3) do not show mRNA changes corresponding with the marked differences in protein levels detected, although some do (S100A2, SNED1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: S100A2 and SNED1 show mRNA changes corresponding with protein level differences.
source: It can be seen that the mRNA changes for several of the proteins of interest (CYR61, EGLN1, LTBP3) do not show mRNA changes corresponding with the marked differences in protein levels detected, although some do (S100A2, SNED1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ltbp3 mRNA is up-regulated during malignant progression in the autochthonous MMTV-PyMT murine mammary tumor model.
source: In addition, we show that Ltbp3 and Sned1 mRNAs are up-regulated during malignant progression in the autochthonous MMTV-PyMT murine mammary tumor model (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Sned1 mRNA is up-regulated during malignant progression in the autochthonous MMTV-PyMT murine mammary tumor model.
source: In addition, we show that Ltbp3 and Sned1 mRNAs are up-regulated during malignant progression in the autochthonous MMTV-PyMT murine mammary tumor model (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: None of the genes (CYR61, LTBP3, SNED1, EGLN1, S100A2), when knocked down, significantly affected primary tumor growth.
source: We observed that none of the genes, when knocked down, significantly affected primary tumor growth (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No differences in tumor cell proliferation or apoptosis were observed between control and knockdown tumors.
source: Consistently, we also observed no differences in tumor cell proliferation or apoptosis between control and knockdown tumors (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The primary tumors and metastases were still ZsGreen-positive, indicating that the shRNA construct was still strongly expressed.
source: Importantly, the primary tumors (and the metastases deriving from them) were still ZsGreen-positive, indicating that the shRNA construct was still strongly expressed (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The knockdowns persisted in vivo.
source: We also confirmed that the knockdowns persisted in vivo (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and that there was no compensatory up-regulation of these genes by the stroma (data not shown).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no compensatory up-regulation of the knocked-down genes by the stroma.
source: We also confirmed that the knockdowns persisted in vivo (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and that there was no compensatory up-regulation of these genes by the stroma (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as confirmed but data not shown.

claim: LM2 cells metastasize to the lungs, liver and spleen from the primary site.
source: We observed that the parental LM2 cells and the LM2 cells expressing the control hairpin, in addition to metastasizing to the lung, also could colonize the liver and the spleen from the primary site (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Knocking down CYR61 did not affect metastasis formation.
source: Whereas knocking down CYR61, a protein that we detected by proteomics in both poorly and highly metastatic tumors, did not affect metastasis formation, knocking down any of the four genes characteristic of highly metastatic (LM2) tumors, and not detected in the poorly metastatic (MDA-MB-231) tumors, led to a significant decrease of the metastatic burden as compared with that of mice injected with control LM2 cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Knocking down LTBP3, SNED1, EGLN1, or S100A2 led to a significant decrease of the metastatic burden.
source: Whereas knocking down CYR61, a protein that we detected by proteomics in both poorly and highly metastatic tumors, did not affect metastasis formation, knocking down any of the four genes characteristic of highly metastatic (LM2) tumors, and not detected in the poorly metastatic (MDA-MB-231) tumors, led to a significant decrease of the metastatic burden as compared with that of mice injected with control LM2 cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and subsequent panels.

claim: None of the SNED1 or EGLN1 knockdown tumors disseminated to organs other than the lungs.
source: None of the SNED1 or EGLN1 knockdown tumors disseminated to organs other than the lungs and the number of mice presenting visible lung metastases was dramatically decreased (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The number of mice presenting visible lung metastases was dramatically decreased for SNED1 and EGLN1 knockdown tumors.
source: None of the SNED1 or EGLN1 knockdown tumors disseminated to organs other than the lungs and the number of mice presenting visible lung metastases was dramatically decreased (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: LTBP3 and S100A2 knockdown led to a very significant inhibition of metastatic dissemination.
source: LTBP3 and S100A2 knockdown also led to a very significant inhibition of metastatic dissemination, although we detected occasional visible metastases in the liver or spleen of mice injected with LTBP3 or S100A2 knockdown cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Occasional visible metastases in the liver or spleen were detected in mice injected with LTBP3 or S100A2 knockdown cells.
source: LTBP3 and S100A2 knockdown also led to a very significant inhibition of metastatic dissemination, although we detected occasional visible metastases in the liver or spleen of mice injected with LTBP3 or S100A2 knockdown cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The four ECM proteins (LTBP3, SNED1, EGLN1, S100A2) play significant functional roles in the metastatic dissemination of mammary tumor cells.
source: These results demonstrate that these four ECM proteins play significant functional roles in the metastatic dissemination of these mammary tumor cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Knock-down of any of the five ECM genes selected did not affect significantly primary tumor vascularization.
source: Knock-down of any of the five ECM genes selected did not affect significantly primary tumor vascularization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Control tumors markedly invaded the skin and surrounding muscles.
source: Control tumors markedly invaded the skin (Figure 6) and the surrounding muscles (not shown), and were significantly fibrotic, as indicated by staining tumor sections with Masson's Trichrome (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: Control tumors were significantly fibrotic.
source: Control tumors markedly invaded the skin (Figure 6) and the surrounding muscles (not shown), and were significantly fibrotic, as indicated by staining tumor sections with Masson's Trichrome (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 with Masson's Trichrome staining.

claim: CYR61, EGLN1, and S100A2 knockdown did not influence tumor invasion or fibrosis.
source: Cells in which CYR61, EGLN1, or S100A2 were knocked down formed highly invasive (white arrow) and desmoplastic tumors resembling the control tumors, suggesting that these proteins did not influence tumor invasion or fibrosis (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: LTBP3 and SNED1 knockdown tumors were characterized by deposition of collagen at the periphery of the tumor forming a thick capsule.
source: Interestingly, LTBP3 and SNED1 knockdown tumors were characterized by deposition of collagen at the periphery of the tumor forming a thick capsule.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: LTBP3 and SNED1 tumors failed to invade the surrounding tissues.
source: Consistently, the LTBP3 and SNED1 tumors failed to invade the surrounding tissues, suggesting that LTBP3 and SNED1 are promoters of tumor invasiveness.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: LTBP3 and SNED1 are promoters of tumor invasiveness.
source: Consistently, the LTBP3 and SNED1 tumors failed to invade the surrounding tissues, suggesting that LTBP3 and SNED1 are promoters of tumor invasiveness.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that knockdown of these proteins resulted in encapsulated, non-invasive tumors.

claim: Control LM2 cells efficiently seeded and colonized the lungs when injected into the blood circulation.
source: When injected into the blood circulation, control LM2 cells efficiently seeded and colonized the lungs and formed large metastases detectable by fluorescence (Figure 7A, upper panel), by staining lung sections with hematoxylin and eosin (Figure 7A, middle panel) or with an anti-human vimentin antibody (Figure 7A, lower panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Knockdown of EGLN1 or S100A2 strongly inhibited the formation of pulmonary metastases.
source: Knockdown of EGLN1 or S100A2 strongly inhibited the formation of pulmonary metastases (Figure 7A–7C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Knockdown of LTBP3 or SNED1 in LM2 cells did not affect lung colonization.
source: In contrast, knockdown of LTBP3 or SNED1 in LM2 cells did not affect lung colonization (Figure 7A,B), consistent with our finding that these proteins influence tumor cell invasion at the primary site (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: LTBP3 knockdown gave rise to the same number of metastases but the metastases were significantly smaller.
source: Although LTBP3 knockdown gave rise to the same number of metastases, the metastases were significantly smaller (based on the size of the ZsGreen-positive foci) and consistently, the Alu PCR signal was significantly lower than in the control lungs (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C.

claim: LTBP3 and SNED1 likely act early in the metastatic cascade by promoting tumor invasiveness.
source: Together, our data suggest that, although all these four proteins are required to increase metastasis formation, they do so by influencing different steps of the metastatic cascade. LTBP3 and SNED1 likely act early in the metastatic cascade by promoting tumor invasiveness.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of orthotopic and tail vein injection experiments.

claim: LTBP3 appears to affect the growth of lung metastases.
source: In addition, LTBP3, but not SNED1, appears to affect the growth of lung metastases.
evidence: This is inferred from the tail vein injection experiments showing smaller metastases with LTBP3 knockdown.

claim: EGLN1 and S100A2 are likely to act at later stages of the metastatic cascade.
source: Our data also suggest that EGLN1 and S100A2 are likely to act at later stages of the metastatic cascade (extravasation, seeding, survival, and/or growth of the tumor cells in secondary sites) because, although the primary tumors are very invasive, they failed to colonize distant organs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these proteins affect metastasis in tail vein injections but not primary tumor invasion.

claim: SNED1 expression inversely correlated with the survival of estrogen-receptor-negative and progesterone-receptor-negative (ER−/PR−) breast cancer patients.
source: Whereas the expression of none of the genes studied correlated with distant metastasis-free survival for the entire population of breast cancer patients, SNED1 and LTBP3 expression inversely correlated with the survival of estrogen-receptor-negative and progesterone-receptor-negative (ER−/PR−) breast cancer patients.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 using Kaplan-Meier Plotter analysis.

claim: LTBP3 expression inversely correlated with the survival of estrogen-receptor-negative and progesterone-receptor-negative (ER−/PR−) breast cancer patients.
source: Whereas the expression of none of the genes studied correlated with distant metastasis-free survival for the entire population of breast cancer patients, SNED1 and LTBP3 expression inversely correlated with the survival of estrogen-receptor-negative and progesterone-receptor-negative (ER−/PR−) breast cancer patients.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8 using Kaplan-Meier Plotter analysis.

claim: A proteomics-based discovery approach can define ECM signatures of tumors of differing metastatic potential.
source: We demonstrate in this study that a proteomics-based discovery approach can define ECM signatures of tumors of differing metastatic potential.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by all the proteomic data.

claim: A high proportion of the proteins detected as up-regulated in highly metastatic tumors contribute to metastatic dissemination.
source: Indeed, a high proportion of the proteins we detected as up-regulated in highly metastatic tumors (some reported previously, some new to this study) contribute to metastatic dissemination.
evidence: This is based on the functional validation experiments and literature citations.

claim: Four out of five ECM or ECM-associated proteins not previously clearly implicated in metastasis play roles at different steps of the metastatic cascade.
source: We studied in detail five ECM or ECM-associated proteins not previously clearly implicated in metastasis and demonstrate that four out of five of these proteins play roles at different steps of the metastatic cascade.
evidence: This is based on the functional experiments with CYR61, LTBP3, SNED1, EGLN1, and S100A2.

claim: CYR61 was up-regulated in more aggressive tumor cell lines or lesions in previous studies.
source: CYR61 was detected in both poorly and highly metastatic tumors but with a greater abundance in highly metastatic tumors. Previous studies had reported the up-regulation of CYR61 in more aggressive tumor cell lines or lesions (Tsai et al., 2000, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tsai et al., 2000, 2002.

claim: Although produced in greater abundance by highly metastatic tumors, CYR61 is not necessary to promote metastatic dissemination.
source: Our study demonstrates that although produced in greater abundance by highly metastatic tumors, CYR61 is not necessary to promote metastatic dissemination as knocking down its expression did not have any effect on the metastatic dissemination of LM2 cells.
evidence: This is based on the knockdown experiments showing no effect on metastasis.

claim: TGFβ plays a role in cancer progression.
source: Consistent with the role of TGFβ in cancer progression (Padua and Massagué, 2009; Massague, 2012), we show that LTBP3, a protein that regulates TGFβ secretion and bioavailability (Chen et al., 2002; Munger and Sheppard, 2011) promotes primary tumor invasion and metastasis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Padua and Massagué, 2009 and Massague, 2012.

claim: LTBP3 is a protein that regulates TGFβ secretion and bioavailability.
source: Consistent with the role of TGFβ in cancer progression (Padua and Massagué, 2009; Massague, 2012), we show that LTBP3, a protein that regulates TGFβ secretion and bioavailability (Chen et al., 2002; Munger and Sheppard, 2011) promotes primary tumor invasion and metastasis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2002 and Munger and Sheppard, 2011.

claim: LTBP3 promotes primary tumor invasion and metastasis.
source: Consistent with the role of TGFβ in cancer progression (Padua and Massagué, 2009; Massague, 2012), we show that LTBP3, a protein that regulates TGFβ secretion and bioavailability (Chen et al., 2002; Munger and Sheppard, 2011) promotes primary tumor invasion and metastasis.
evidence: This is based on the knockdown experiments showing reduced invasion and metastasis.

claim: LTBP3 is a protein that contributes to the formation of the fibrillar ECM network.
source: LTBP3 is also a protein that contributes to the formation of the fibrillar ECM network (Ramirez and Rifkin, 2009; Todorovic and Rifkin, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ramirez and Rifkin, 2009 and Todorovic and Rifkin, 2012.

claim: LTBP1, LTBP2, and LTBP4 were all detected in the matrisome of both poorly and highly metastatic tumors.
source: Of note, LTBP3 is a member of a family of proteins and the three other members of the family; LTBP1, LTBP2 and LTBP4 were all detected in the matrisome of both poorly and highly metastatic tumors, LTBP1 and 4 being expressed by the tumor cells and not the stromal cells and LTBP2 being expressed by both the tumor cells and stromal cells (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: LTBP1 and LTBP4 are expressed by the tumor cells and not the stromal cells.
source: Of note, LTBP3 is a member of a family of proteins and the three other members of the family; LTBP1, LTBP2 and LTBP4 were all detected in the matrisome of both poorly and highly metastatic tumors, LTBP1 and 4 being expressed by the tumor cells and not the stromal cells and LTBP2 being expressed by both the tumor cells and stromal cells (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: LTBP2 is expressed by both the tumor cells and stromal cells.
source: Of note, LTBP3 is a member of a family of proteins and the three other members of the family; LTBP1, LTBP2 and LTBP4 were all detected in the matrisome of both poorly and highly metastatic tumors, LTBP1 and 4 being expressed by the tumor cells and not the stromal cells and LTBP2 being expressed by both the tumor cells and stromal cells (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: SNED1 is a large ECM glycoprotein first identified as a potential component of the basement membrane.
source: SNED1 (Sushi, Nidogen, and EGF-like Domains 1) is a large ECM glycoprotein first identified as a potential component of the basement membrane (Leimeister et al., 2004) whose roles in normal physiology and pathology remain to be characterized.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leimeister et al., 2004.

claim: This study reports for the first time a functional role for SNED1 in tumor progression and metastasis.
source: In this study, we report for the first time a functional role for SNED1 in tumor progression and metastasis and we now wish to understand the molecular mechanisms by which SNED1 contributes to tumor progression.
evidence: This is based on the functional experiments showing SNED1 knockdown reduces metastasis.

claim: SNED1 displays two potential integrin-binding sites: an RGD motif upstream of the amino-terminal NIDO domain and an LDV motif upstream of the first EGF domain.
source: Interestingly, SNED1 displays two potential integrin-binding sites, an RGD motif is found upstream of the amino-terminal NIDO domain and an LDV motif is upstream of the first EGF domain.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of SNED1.

claim: EGLN1 is a prolyl-hydroxylase that catalyzes the hydroxylation of proline residues of HIF1α in normoxic conditions.
source: EGLN1 (also known as PHD2, Prolyl Hydroxylase Domain-containing protein 2) is a prolyl-hydroxylase and, in normoxic conditions, catalyzes the hydroxylation of proline residues of the hypoxia-inducible factor 1 α (HIF1α), rendering it susceptible to poly-ubiquitinylation and subsequent proteasomal degradation (Berra et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berra et al., 2003.

claim: Hydroxylation of HIF1α by EGLN1 renders it susceptible to poly-ubiquitinylation and subsequent proteasomal degradation.
source: EGLN1 (also known as PHD2, Prolyl Hydroxylase Domain-containing protein 2) is a prolyl-hydroxylase and, in normoxic conditions, catalyzes the hydroxylation of proline residues of the hypoxia-inducible factor 1 α (HIF1α), rendering it susceptible to poly-ubiquitinylation and subsequent proteasomal degradation (Berra et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berra et al., 2003.

claim: Inhibiting EGLN1 had an anti-tumor effect by enhancing TGFβ anti-proliferative effect in a model of murine osteosarcoma.
source: Klotsche-van Ameln et al. have reported that inhibiting EGLN1 had an anti-tumor effect by enhancing TGFβ anti-proliferative effect in a model of murine osteosarcoma (Klotzsche-von Ameln et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Klotzsche-von Ameln et al., 2011.

claim: S100A2 is a calcium-binding protein that belongs to the S100 family of acute-phase response factors.
source: S100A2 is a calcium-binding protein that belongs to the S100 family of acute-phase response factors and, when overexpressed in non-small-cell lung carcinoma cells subsequently injected subcutaneously in mice, has been shown to promote metastasis to the lungs (Bulk et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about S100A2.

claim: S100A2, when overexpressed in non-small-cell lung carcinoma cells subsequently injected subcutaneously in mice, has been shown to promote metastasis to the lungs.
source: S100A2 is a calcium-binding protein that belongs to the S100 family of acute-phase response factors and, when overexpressed in non-small-cell lung carcinoma cells subsequently injected subcutaneously in mice, has been shown to promote metastasis to the lungs (Bulk et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bulk et al., 2009.

claim: S100A2 is important for the growth of tumor cells in distant organs, in particular the lungs.
source: The fact that we observed a decrease in the number of metastases formed by cells in which S100A2 was knockeddown, both when the cells were injected orthotopically and metastasized from the primary tumor and when the cells were injected in the circulation, suggests that S100A2 is important for the growth of tumor cells in distant organs, in particular the lungs.
evidence: This is inferred from the knockdown experiments in both orthotopic and tail vein injection models.

claim: The proteomics-based discovery pipeline identified proteins playing a causal role in tumor progression and metastatic dissemination with high yield.
source: The proteomics-based discovery pipeline we developed identified, with high yield, proteins playing a causal role in tumor progression and metastatic dissemination.
evidence: This is based on the fact that 4 out of 5 tested proteins showed functional roles.

claim: ADAM9 and ADAM10 have been implicated in invasiveness of breast tumor cells in previous studies.
source: Indeed, in addition to the four proteins whose involvement in mammary carcinoma metastasis we report here, previous studies using various mammary carcinoma cell lines or tumor models had already implicated several other proteins in breast cancer progression (ANGPTL4, CTSB, IGFBP4, LOXL2) or invasiveness of breast tumor cells (ADAM9, ADAM10).
evidence: This is stated as previous knowledge from the literature.

claim: ADAM9, LOXL2, and S100A2 show statistically significant correlations with poor prognosis for metastasis-free survival of breast cancer patients.
source: In addition, analyses by Kaplan–Meier Plotter (Györffy et al., 2010) show that several proteins from our list of ECM proteins up-regulated in highly metastatic LM2 cells (ADAM9, LOXL2, S100A2; data not shown) show statistically significant correlations with poor prognosis for metastasis-free survival of breast cancer patients.
evidence: This is based on Kaplan-Meier Plotter analysis.

claim: From the list of 43 ECM proteins expressed only in metastatic LM2 cells, 12 show suggestive evidence of functional involvement in metastasis of breast cancer.
source: Thus, in total, from the list of 43 ECM proteins that we find expressed only in the metastatic LM2 cells and not in MDA-MB-231, 12 show suggestive evidence of functional involvement in metastasis of breast cancer.
evidence: This is a summary of the functional validation and literature evidence.

claim: CTGF, TIMP1, and S100A10 have been previously implicated in tumor progression in other cancer types.
source: Also included are proteins previously implicated in tumor progression in other cancer types (e.g., CTGF, TIMP1, S100A10) and proteins that we have identified in proteomics screens of other tumor models (unpublished data).
evidence: This is stated as previous knowledge from the literature.

claim: The proteins identified in this study are relevant to breast cancer metastasis and their significance is likely not limited solely to the breast cancer lines used in this study.
source: These concordances indicate that the proteins we identify here are relevant to breast cancer metastasis and their significance is likely not limited solely to the breast cancer lines we used in this study.
evidence: This is inferred from the concordance with literature and patient data.

claim: The miR-200 family has been identified in breast cancer patients as being pro-metastatic via its inhibition of Sec23a.
source: Korpal et al. have identified in breast cancer patients the miR-200 family as being pro-metastatic via its inhibition of Sec23a, a protein involved in the secretion machinery (Korpal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Korpal et al., 2011.

claim: AGRN, LTBP3, EFEMP2, IGFBP4, SERPINE2, SNED1 and TINAGL1 were shown to be down-regulated in the conditioned medium of Sec23a knockdown cells.
source: Interestingly, several of the proteins we found to be up-regulated in highly metastatic tumors (AGRN, LTBP3, EFEMP2, IGFBP4, SERPINE2, SNED1 and TINAGL1) were shown in the Korpal study to be down-regulated in the conditioned medium of Sec23a knockdown cells and were thus postulated to be anti-metastatic.
evidence: This is based on the Korpal et al. study.

claim: The set of proteins (AGRN, LTBP3, EFEMP2, IGFBP4, SERPINE2, SNED1 and TINAGL1) is pro-metastatic according to this study.
source: However, our study indicates that this set of proteins is pro-metastatic, which could point towards tumor-specific or context-dependent mechanisms of action for these proteins.
evidence: This is based on the functional data from this study.

claim: Not only the production of tumor-derived ECM proteins changes with a tumor's metastatic potential but the stromal contribution to the tumor ECM also changes.
source: Our study also revealed that not only the production of tumor-derived ECM proteins changes with a tumor's metastatic potential but the stromal contribution to the tumor ECM also changes.
evidence: This is based on the species-specific peptide analysis.

claim: The composition of the stroma of a non-metastatic primary tumor differs from that of a highly metastatic primary tumor.
source: This is consistent with the idea that the composition of the stroma (possibly including the cell types present) of a non-metastatic primary tumor differs from that of a highly metastatic primary tumor and that tumor cells of different metastatic potential may recruit different stromal cell types.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that stroma-derived ECM proteins differ between tumor types.

claim: LM2 tumors are more vascularized than the MDA-MB-231 tumors.
source: In fact, we have observed that LM2 tumors are more vascularized than the MDA-MB-231 tumors (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation but data not shown.

claim: Tumor cells of different metastatic potential can instruct local stromal cells to express different sets of ECM proteins.
source: Our data also suggest that tumor cells of different metastatic potential can instruct local stromal cells to express different sets of ECM proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that stroma-derived ECM proteins differ between tumor types.

claim: Cancer-associated fibroblasts from different mammary tumor subtypes differ in their expression profiles.
source: This interesting aspect of tumor–stroma interactions has not been extensively studied in vivo, although a recent paper notes that cancer-associated fibroblasts from different mammary tumor subtypes differ in their expression profiles (Tchou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tchou et al., 2012.

claim: ECM proteins are favorable candidate biomarkers since they are abundant, are laid down in characteristic patterns and are readily accessible.
source: ECM proteins are particularly favorable candidate biomarkers since they are abundant, are laid down in characteristic patterns and are readily accessible.
evidence: This is a general statement about the properties of ECM proteins.

claim: ECM proteins can serve as anchors to deliver selectively to tumors and/or metastases imaging probes to enhance the detection of metastases or anti-tumor agents to enhance therapy.
source: ECM proteins can also serve as anchors to deliver selectively to tumors and/or metastases imaging probes to enhance the detection of metastases or anti-tumor agents to enhance therapy on the model of the work pioneered by Neri et al. (Pasche and Neri, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pasche and Neri, 2012.

claim: The proteins discovered in the differential proteomics-based approach have the potential to serve as novel anticancer therapeutic targets.
source: Finally, another possible translational aspect is the identification of potential novel direct therapeutic targets. Whether by targeting the interactions between ECM proteins and their cellular receptors (Goodman and Picard, 2012) or by disrupting the architecture of the ECM (that acts as a barrier) to allow more efficient drug delivery (Yuan et al., 2007; Whatcott et al., 2011; Jacobetz et al., 2013), the proteins discovered in our differential proteomics-based approach have the potential to serve as novel anticancer therapeutic targets.
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant studies and is speculative about future applications.
